claim: siRNA-mediated knockdown of IRSp53 gene expression induces a decrease in viral particle production.
source: siRNA-mediated knockdown of IRSp53 gene expression induces a decrease in viral particle production and a viral bud arrest at half completion.
evidence: The abstract directly states this finding, which is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: siRNA-mediated knockdown of IRSp53 gene expression induces a viral bud arrest at half completion.
source: siRNA-mediated knockdown of IRSp53 gene expression induces a decrease in viral particle production and a viral bud arrest at half completion.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, supported by electron microscopy data in Figure 1c-e showing arrested buds.

claim: IRSp53 shows preferential localization around HIV-1 Gag assembly sites at the cell plasma membrane.
source: Single-molecule localization microscopy at the cell plasma membrane shows a preferential localization of IRSp53 around HIV-1 Gag assembly sites.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by PALM/STORM microscopy data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: IRSp53 is present in purified HIV-1 particles.
source: In addition, we observe the presence of IRSp53 in purified HIV-1 particles.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, supported by immunoblot data in Figure 5c-e showing IRSp53 in purified viral particles.

claim: HIV-1 Gag protein preferentially localizes to curved membranes induced by IRSp53 I-BAR domain on giant unilamellar vesicles.
source: Finally, HIV-1 Gag protein preferentially localizes to curved membranes induced by IRSp53 I-BAR domain on giant unilamellar vesicles.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, supported by GUV experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: IRSp53 is a crucial host factor in HIV-1 membrane curvature.
source: This highlights IRSp53 as a crucial host factor in HIV-1 membrane curvature and its requirement for full HIV-1 particle assembly.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental findings including knockdown, localization, and in vitro studies.

claim: IRSp53 is required for full HIV-1 particle assembly.
source: This highlights IRSp53 as a crucial host factor in HIV-1 membrane curvature and its requirement for full HIV-1 particle assembly.
evidence: This conclusion is supported by knockdown experiments showing arrested assembly and reduced particle release.

claim: Partial knockdown of IRSp53 expression reduces HIV-1 particle release threefold in Jurkat T cells.
source: Partial IRSp53 gene expression knockdown (resulting in a maximum of 50% protein depletion) reduced particle release threefold as compared to the control siRNA (Figure 1a, bottom), and a sixfold reduction was determined when taking into account the percentage of protein depletion.
evidence: This is directly stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative data in Figure 1a.

claim: The reduction in HIV-1 particle release upon IRSp53 knockdown is highly significant (p value = 0.00265).
source: This reduction in HIV-1 particle release is highly significant (n = 3 independent experiments, p value = 0.00265, Student's t-test, and ANOVA statistical test for multiple comparisons indicate p value = 0.0089)
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data from Figure 1a.

claim: Partial knockdown of IRSp53 (~50% protein depletion) resulted in a two- to threefold decrease in HIV-1 Gag particle production in HEK293T cells.
source: Partial knockdown of IRSp53 (~50% protein depletion) resulted in a two- to threefold decrease in HIV-1 Gag particle production (n = 3 independent experiments, p value = 0.000487, Student's t-test) (Figure 1b, bottom, Figure 1—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1b.

claim: Knockdown of IRTKS did not have any significant effect on HIV Gag particle release.
source: In contrast, knockdown of IRTKS (Figure 1b, Figure 1—figure supplement 1e) did not have any significant effect on HIV Gag particle release (n = 3 independent experiments, p value = 0.0924, Student's t-test)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1b.

claim: IRTKS does not have redundant functions with IRSp53 in the context of HIV-1 Gag particle formation.
source: thus precluding the possibility of redundant functions between IRSp53 and IRTKS in the context of HIV-1 Gag particle formation.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the differential effects of IRSp53 vs IRTKS knockdown on particle release.

claim: IRSp53 knockdown cells displayed arrested buds at an early assembly stage.
source: While control cells displayed a range of HIV-1 Gag particles at different stages of assembly and budding, the cells knocked down for IRSp53 instead displayed arrested buds at an early assembly stage (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by electron microscopy images in Figure 1d.

claim: Buds from cells knocked down for IRSp53 displayed a narrower range of curvature height (48 ± 22 nm) compared to control (85 ± 53 nm).
source: By measuring the dimensions of these arrested buds, we found that buds from cells knocked down for IRSp53 displayed a narrower range of curvature height (48 ± 22 nm), as compared to the control (85 ± 53 nm) (n = 145 buds from 14 different cells, p value = 1.053 × 10−28, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 1e.

claim: The bud widths presented no difference between siIRSp53 (135 ± 64 nm) and the control (140 ± 87 nm).
source: while the bud widths presented no difference between siIRSp53 (135 ± 64 nm) and the control (140 ± 87 nm) (n = 145 buds from 14 different cells, p value = 0.0609, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test) (Figure 1e).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 1e.

claim: In the absence of IRSp53, viral buds were unable to progress beyond a certain curvature.
source: The result indicates that in the absence of IRSp53, the viral buds were unable to progress beyond a certain curvature.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the bud dimension measurements showing arrested buds at a specific height.

claim: HIV-1 Gag and endogenous IRSp53 are components of the same intracellular complex.
source: We then concluded that HIV-1 Gag and endogenous IRSp53, or ectopic IRSp53-GFP, were components of the same intracellular complex, interacting directly or indirectly through other factors or membrane domains.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 2a,b.

claim: IP of endogenous IRSp53 resulted in co-precipitation of Gag.
source: Our results showed that IP of endogenous IRSp53 resulted in co-precipitation of Gag (Figure 2a, lane 1), as compared to the controls (lanes 2–4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 2a.

claim: IP of ectopic IRSp53-GFP with an anti-GFP antibody resulted in co-precipitation of Gag.
source: To overcome this issue, we performed an IP/co-IP experiment of ectopic IRSp53-GFP/HIV-1 Gag proteins with an anti-GFP antibody, and confirmed the pull-down of IRSp53-GFP (Figure 2b, lanes 2 and 3) and the co-precipitation of Gag (lane 3) while nothing was detected in the controls (lanes 1 and 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 2b.

claim: At equilibrium, 19 ± 8% of IRSp53 was bound to the cell membranes in the absence of Gag.
source: Thus, at equilibrium, 19 ± 8% of IRSp53 was bound to the cell membranes (Graph, Figure 2d).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by membrane flotation assay data in Figure 2d.

claim: 66 ± 9% of Gag was bound to the cell membranes in cells expressing HIV-1 Gag.
source: The same experiment was repeated with cells expressing HIV-1 Gag, where 66 ± 9% of Gag was bound to the cell membranes (Graph, Figure 2d).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by membrane flotation assay data in Figure 2d.

claim: There was a twofold increase in IRSp53 bound to the cell membranes upon HIV-1 Gag expression (44 ± 5%).
source: Notably, we observed a twofold increase with 44 ± 5% of IRSp53 bound to the cell membranes upon HIV-1 Gag expression (Graph Figure 2d) (n = 5 independent experiments, p value = 0.000129, Student's t-test), while none with IRTKS.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by membrane flotation assay data in Figure 2d.

claim: There was a twofold increase in cell membrane binding of Tsg101 upon Gag expression, passing from 36 ± 10% without Gag to 79 ± 8% in the presence of Gag.
source: Here, we observe a twofold increase in cell membrane binding of Tsg101 upon Gag expression, passing from 36 ± 10% without Gag to 79 ± 8% in the presence of Gag (Figure 2c) (n = 5 independent experiments, p value = 0.00517, Student's t-test).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by membrane flotation assay data in Figure 2c.

claim: Gag, Gag(i)mEos2, and GagΔp6(i)mEos2 were all pulled down with IRSp53.
source: Our experiments revealed that Gag, Gag(i)mEos2, and GagΔp6(i)mEos2 were all pulled down with IRSp53 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The addition of the internal mEos2 protein did not affect the complexation of Gag with IRSp53.
source: showing that the addition of the internal mEos2 protein - a necessary tag for super resolution microscopy (SRM) imaging of Gag (see the following section) - did not affect the complexation of Gag with IRSp53.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the immunoprecipitation data showing similar pull-down of Gag and Gag(i)mEos2 with IRSp53.

claim: The p6 domain was not required for Gag/IRSp53 molecular interplay.
source: Moreover, we showed that the p6 domain was not required for Gag/IRSp53 molecular interplay suggesting that it occurs before ESCRT recruitment.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the immunoprecipitation data showing GagΔp6 still co-precipitates with IRSp53.

claim: 27% of all IRSp53 localizations are highly correlated with Gag(i)mEos2 localizations (CBC >0.5) in HEK293T cells.
source: IRSp53 CBC distribution (c) shows that 27% of all IRSp53 localizations are highly correlated with Gag(i)mEos2 localizations (>0.5).
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 3c and supported by coordinate-based colocalization analysis.

claim: Only 14% of IRTKS localizations are highly correlated with Gag(i)mEos2 localizations (CBC >0.5) in HEK293T cells.
source: On the other hand, only 14% of IRTKS localizations (d) are highly correlated, while IRTKS CBC distribution exhibits a peak of anti-correlated/non-correlated (−0.5 to 0) localization.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 3d and supported by coordinate-based colocalization analysis.

claim: 26% of IRSp53 localizations are highly correlated with Gag(i)mEos2 localizations (CBC >0.5) in Jurkat T cells.
source: (g) shows that 26% of IRSp53 localizations are highly correlated with Gag(i)mEos2 localizations (>0.5)
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 3g and supported by coordinate-based colocalization analysis.

claim: IRSp53 displays stronger single-molecule colocalization with Gag in assembling clusters than IRTKS does.
source: This comparison directly shows that IRSp53 displays stronger single-molecule colocalization with Gag in assembling clusters than IRTKS does.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the CBC analysis comparing IRSp53 and IRTKS colocalization with Gag.

claim: IRSp53 localization displays a restricted pattern around and in the assembly sites, corresponding to a circular ring surrounding the assembly site at 80 nm from the center of the Gag budding sites with a width of 80 nm.
source: This comparison indicated that IRSp53 localization, on average, displays a restricted pattern around and in the assembly sites. This corresponds to a circular ring surrounding the assembly site at 80 nm from the center of the Gag budding sites with a width of 80 nm (Figure 4c,e).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by simulation analysis comparing experimental and simulated CBC distributions in Figure 4.

claim: IRTKS was present as a large diffuse pattern located at 140 nm from the Gag assembly site center with a width of 200 nm.
source: On the other hand, IRTKS was present as a large diffuse pattern located at 140 nm from the Gag assembly site center with a width of 200 nm, explaining why fewer IRTKS molecules were detected in the assembly sites (Figure 4d,f).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by simulation analysis comparing experimental and simulated CBC distributions in Figure 4.

claim: IRSp53 specifically localizes at HIV-1 Gag assembly sites at the cell plasma membrane, whereas IRTKS poorly does.
source: Our results thus show that IRSp53 indeed specifically localizes at HIV-1 Gag assembly sites at the cell plasma membrane, whereas IRTKS poorly does.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the PALM/STORM imaging and CBC analysis showing differential localization patterns of IRSp53 vs IRTKS.

claim: IRSp53-GFP shows high correlation (Mander's coefficient = 0.95–1) with Gag-mCherry VLPs.
source: We found a high correlation (Mander's coefficient = 0.95–1) between IRSp53-GFP and Gag-mCherry (Figure 5b, left graph, red column), indicating that almost all Gag-mCherry VLPs contained IRSp53-GFP
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by colocalization analysis of purified VLPs in Figure 5b.

claim: Almost all Gag-mCherry VLPs contained IRSp53-GFP.
source: We found a high correlation (Mander's coefficient = 0.95–1) between IRSp53-GFP and Gag-mCherry (Figure 5b, left graph, red column), indicating that almost all Gag-mCherry VLPs contained IRSp53-GFP
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by colocalization analysis of purified VLPs in Figure 5b.

claim: When using the IRSp53-I-BAR domain alone, a high Mander's coefficient of ~0.8 was obtained.
source: When using the IRSp53-I-BAR domain alone, we also obtained a high Mander's coefficient, that is, ~0.8 (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by colocalization analysis of purified VLPs in Figure 5b.

claim: For IRTKS-GFP, the Mander's coefficient was 0.4–0.5, indicating no significant correlation between IRTKS-GFP and Gag-mCherry.
source: In contrast, for IRTKS-GFP, the Mander's coefficient was 0.4–0.5, indicating no significant correlation between IRTKS-GFP and Gag-mCherry.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by colocalization analysis of purified VLPs in Figure 5b.

claim: Even if a domain (PH-PLCδ) or another I-BAR protein (IRTKS) can recognize PI(4,5)P2 at the cell membrane, it is not sufficient for incorporation into Gag-VLPs.
source: This indicates that even if a domain (PH-PLCδ) or another I-BAR protein (IRTKS) can recognize PI(4,5)P2 at the cell membrane, it is not sufficient for incorporation into Gag-VLPs.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the differential incorporation of IRSp53 vs IRTKS and PH-PLCδ into VLPs.

claim: Endogenous IRSp53 was found to be associated with the viral particles in both infectious HIV-1 and Gag VLPs.
source: IRSp53 was found to be associated with the viral particles in both conditions, that is, in infectious HIV-1 and in Gag VLPs, indicating that Gag alone is sufficient to recruit IRSp53 in the viral particles (Figure 5c,d, 'IRSp53').
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 5c,d.

claim: Gag alone is sufficient to recruit IRSp53 in the viral particles.
source: IRSp53 was found to be associated with the viral particles in both conditions, that is, in infectious HIV-1 and in Gag VLPs, indicating that Gag alone is sufficient to recruit IRSp53 in the viral particles (Figure 5c,d, 'IRSp53').
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation that IRSp53 is present in both full HIV-1 and Gag-only VLPs.

claim: IRTKS was not associated neither with Gag-VLP nor HIV-1 particles.
source: In contrast, IRTKS was not associated neither with Gag-VLP nor HIV-1 particles (Figure 5c,d, 'IRTKS').
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 5c,d.

claim: IRSp53 and the ESCRT proteins Tsg101 and ALIX were found to be associated within the same fractions containing the HIV-1 Gag viral particles.
source: Upon further purification (Figure 5e), IRSp53, and the ESCRT proteins, Tsg101 and ALIX, were found to be associated within the same fractions containing the HIV-1 Gag viral particles, together with other well-known viral particle cofactors such as CD81, CD63 tetraspanins (Grigorov et al., 2009; Grigorov et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by iodixanol gradient fractionation data in Figure 5e.

claim: Endogenous IRSp53 is most probably incorporated in HIV-1 particles in a Gag-dependent manner.
source: Thus, endogenous IRSp53 is most probably incorporated in HIV-1 particles in a Gag-dependent manner.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation that IRSp53 is found in purified viral particles and co-fractionates with Gag.

claim: Gag binding to GUV membranes is increased ~7-fold when IRSp53-I-BAR domain was introduced first on GUVs before adding Gag (median value 6.7), compared to the condition of Gag only (median value 0.9).
source: We found that Gag binding to GUV membranes is increased ~7-fold when IRSp53-I-BAR domain was introduced first on GUVs before adding Gag (median value 6.7), compared to the condition of Gag only (median value 0.9) (p <0.0001, Student's t-test) (Figure 6a, 'Gag only' vs. 'I-BAR + Gag').
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by GUV binding assay data in Figure 6a.

claim: In the condition where Gag was introduced before adding the I-BAR domain, Gag intensity on GUV membranes increased only ~3-fold as compared to the Gag only condition.
source: However, in the condition where Gag was introduced before adding the I-BAR domain, Gag intensity on GUV membranes increased only ~3-fold as compared to the Gag only condition (p < 0.0001, Student's t-test) (Figure 6a, 'Gag only' vs. 'Gag + I-BAR').
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by GUV binding assay data in Figure 6a.

claim: By comparing I-BAR + Gag and Gag + I-BAR conditions, there was a twofold higher Gag intensity on GUV membranes in the first condition.
source: Notably, by comparing I-BAR + Gag and Gag + I-BAR conditions, we observed a twofold higher Gag intensity on GUV membranes in the first condition (p < 0.0001, Student's t-test) (Figure 6a, 'I-BAR + Gag' vs. 'Gag + I-BAR').
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by GUV binding assay data in Figure 6a.

claim: IRSp53 I-BAR domain facilitates Gag membrane binding on GUV in favor of increasing Gag concentration locally.
source: Taken together, these results show that IRSp53 I-BAR domain facilitates Gag membrane binding on GUV in favor of increasing Gag concentration locally.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the GUV binding assays showing increased Gag binding in the presence of I-BAR domain.

claim: There was a ~1.5-fold increase of the membrane binding of IRSp53 I-BAR domain in the presence of HIV-1 Gag on GUVs.
source: Consistent with our cell experiment results, we observed a similar increase of the membrane binding (~1.5-fold) of IRSp53 I-BAR domain in the presence of HIV-1 Gag on GUVs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a,b)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by GUV binding assay data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1a,b.

claim: Gag was sorted preferentially to the tips of the tubes generated by the IRSp53 I-BAR domain.
source: This experiment revealed that Gag was sorted preferentially to the tips of the tubes generated by the IRSp53 I-BAR domain (Figure 6b,c,d, Video 1 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1c,d).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by confocal microscopy images of GUVs in Figure 6b,c,d.

claim: For all the tubes (17 tubes), the Gag signal was exclusively located at the tips of the tubes.
source: Moreover, for tubes that were not moving too fast, we found that for all the tubes (17 tubes, protein concentrations: 0.05 μM unlabeled I-BAR domain and 0.3 μM AX488 Gag), the Gag signal was exclusively located at the tips of the tubes (Figure 6d and Video 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by confocal microscopy images in Figure 6d.

claim: Addition of HIV-1 Gag resulted in the formation of shorter I-BAR tubules as compared to GUVs incubated with the IRSp53-I-BAR domain alone.
source: Finally, we observed that addition of HIV-1 Gag resulted in the formation of shorter I-BAR tubules as compared to GUVs incubated with the IRSp53-I-BAR domain alone (Figure 6—figure supplement 1c,d), indicating an interference in I-BAR tubule elongation when Gag sorted to the tubule tips
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by confocal microscopy images in Figure 6—figure supplement 1c,d.

claim: Gag usurps the IRSp53 tubulation function.
source: indicating an interference in I-BAR tubule elongation when Gag sorted to the tubule tips, suggesting that Gag usurps the IRSp53 tubulation function.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation that Gag addition results in shorter I-BAR tubules.

claim: The structural Gag polyprotein of HIV-1, by itself, is responsible for particle assembly.
source: The structural Gag polyprotein of HIV-1, by itself, is responsible for particle assembly (Gheysen et al., 1989)
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Gag can oligomerize at the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane forming virus-like particles (VLPs).
source: and it can oligomerize at the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane forming virus-like particles (VLPs).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as established knowledge about Gag behavior.

claim: The force required to bend the membrane to achieve VLP formation has been proposed to be provided by Gag self-assembly.
source: The force required to bend the membrane to achieve VLP formation has been proposed to be provided by Gag self-assembly (Hurley et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The self-assembly of Gag has been shown to segregate specific lipids.
source: The self-assembly of Gag has also been recently shown to segregate specific lipids (Favard et al., 2019; Yandrapalli et al., 2016)
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The self-assembly of Gag has been shown to segregate specific proteins.
source: and proteins (Sengupta et al., 2019), generating plasma membrane domains that could favor budding (Foret, 2014; Lipowsky, 1993).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Only a small proportion of Gag-initiated clusters reach the fully assembled state leading to VLP release in living CD4+ T cells.
source: However, only a small proportion of Gag-initiated clusters reach the fully assembled state leading to VLP release in living CD4+ T cells (Floderer et al., 2018), while a majority of these clusters lead to aborted events.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: A coarse-grained model of HIV assembly has shown that the self-assembly of Gag might not be sufficient to overcome the energy barrier associated with full viral bud formation.
source: Recently, a coarse-grained model of HIV assembly has shown that the self-assembly of Gag might not be sufficient to overcome this energy barrier (Pak et al., 2017), leaving the assembly in intermediate states.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Other factors may be necessary to assist Gag self-assembly during the generation of new VLPs.
source: This supports the fact that other factors may be necessary to assist Gag self-assembly during the generation of new VLPs.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as an inference from the coarse-grained modeling results.

claim: I-BAR domain proteins sense and induce negative membrane curvature at the nanometer scale.
source: For example, I-BAR domain proteins sense and induce negative membrane curvature at the nanometer scale (a few tens to one hundred nanometers), that is, in the HIV-1 particle diameter size range
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as established knowledge about I-BAR proteins.

claim: I-BAR domain proteins generate outward micrometer-scale membrane protrusions such as membrane ruffles, lamellipodia, and filopodia.
source: while generating outward micrometer-scale membrane protrusions such as membrane ruffles, lamellipodia, and filopodia.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as established knowledge about I-BAR proteins.

claim: IRSp53 was first discovered as a substrate phosphorylated downstream of the insulin receptor.
source: IRSp53 was first discovered as a substrate phosphorylated downstream of the insulin receptor (Yeh et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: IRSp53 is the founding member of the membrane curving I-BAR domain protein family.
source: It is also the founding member of the membrane curving I-BAR domain protein family, whose other mammalian members are MIM (missing-in-metastasis), ABBA (actin-bundling protein with BAIAP2 homology), PinkBAR (planar intestinal and kidney-specific BAR domain protein), and IRTKS (insulin receptor tyrosine kinase substrate) (Zhao et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: IRTKS displays functional redundancy with IRSp53 in being able to curve membranes.
source: The latter, IRTKS, displays functional redundancy with IRSp53 (Chou et al., 2017; Millard et al., 2007) in being able to curve membranes.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: IRSp53 binds both Rac1 through its N-terminal I-BAR domain.
source: In addition to interactions with the plasma membrane, IRSp53 binds both Rac1 through its N-terminal I-BAR domain (Miki et al., 2000)
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: IRSp53 binds Cdc42 directly through its unconventional CRIB domain.
source: and Cdc42 directly through its unconventional CRIB domain (Krugmann et al., 2001)
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Downstream effectors of Rac1/Cdc42 such as WAVE2, Mena, Eps8, and mDia can bind IRSp53 through the SH3 domain.
source: and also downstream effectors of these GTPases such as WAVE2, Mena, Eps8, and mDia can bind IRSp53 through the SH3 domain.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as established knowledge about IRSp53 interactions.

claim: IRSp53 functions as a scaffold protein for the Rac1/Cdc42 cascade.
source: Thus, IRSp53 functions as a scaffold protein for the Rac1/Cdc42 cascade (Scita et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: IRSp53 was reported to exhibit a closed inactive conformation that opens synergistically upon binding to Rac1/Cdc42 and effector proteins.
source: IRSp53 was reported to exhibit a closed inactive conformation that opens synergistically upon binding to Rac1/Cdc42 and effector proteins (Disanza et al., 2013; Kast et al., 2014; Miki and Takenawa, 2002; Suetsugu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Regulation of IRSp53 activity was shown to occur through its phosphorylation and interaction with 14-3-3.
source: Regulation of IRSp53 activity was recently shown to occur through its phosphorylation and interaction with 14-3-3 (Kast and Dominguez, 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The I-BAR domain of IRSp53 is composed of a rigid six alpha-helix bundle dimer that is crescent-shaped.
source: Structurally, the I-BAR domain of IRSp53 is composed of a rigid six alpha-helix bundle dimer that is crescent-shaped.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as established structural knowledge about IRSp53.

claim: Due to its concave membrane-binding surface and lipid interactions, IRSp53 is able to generate negative membrane curvature.
source: Due to its concave membrane-binding surface and lipid interactions, IRSp53 is able to generate negative membrane curvature (Zhao et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: IRSp53 is capable of forming homo-dimers.
source: While capable of forming homo-dimers, IRSp53 is also able to recruit and form hetero-dimers with other proteins to form clusters for the initiation of membrane curvature (Disanza et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: IRSp53 is able to recruit and form hetero-dimers with other proteins to form clusters for the initiation of membrane curvature.
source: While capable of forming homo-dimers, IRSp53 is also able to recruit and form hetero-dimers with other proteins to form clusters for the initiation of membrane curvature (Disanza et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The Rac1/IRSp53/Wave2/Arp2/3 signaling pathway is involved in the release of HIV-1 particles.
source: Since the Rac1/IRSp53/Wave2/Arp2/3 signaling pathway is involved in the release of HIV-1 particles (Thomas et al., 2015)
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Both Gag and IRSp53 target the cell plasma membrane upon interaction with PI(4,5)P2.
source: Since both Gag and IRSp53 target the cell plasma membrane upon interaction with PI(4,5)P2 (Favard et al., 2019; Mattila et al., 2007; Prévost et al., 2015; Saarikangas et al., 2009; Sengupta et al., 2019; Takemura et al., 2017; Yandrapalli et al., 2016)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: BAR domain proteins induce strong PI(4,5)P2 clusters.
source: Indeed, BAR domain proteins, in general, and IRSp53 in particular, are known to induce strong PI(4,5)P2 clusters (Saarikangas et al., 2009; Zhao et al., 2013)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: PI(4,5)P2 plays a role in Gag binding to the cell plasma membrane.
source: PI(4,5)P2 was shown to play a role in Gag binding to the cell plasma membrane (Ono et al., 2004)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: PI(4,5)P2 is strongly clustered during virus assembly.
source: as well as PI(4,5)P2 is strongly clustered during virus assembly (Favard et al., 2019; Ono et al., 2004; Yandrapalli et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Gag cellular expression triggers Rac1 activation.
source: We have previously shown that Gag cellular expression triggers Rac1 activation (Thomas et al., 2015), on which IRSp53 membrane localization and function are dependent.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: IRSp53 membrane localization and function are dependent on Rac1 activation.
source: We have previously shown that Gag cellular expression triggers Rac1 activation (Thomas et al., 2015), on which IRSp53 membrane localization and function are dependent.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as established knowledge about IRSp53.

claim: HIV-1 particles are known to incorporate a large number of cellular proteins, many of which are directly involved in virus budding.

claim: Gag could activate IRSp53 through Rac1 activation.
source: Thus, here, we compared the relative membrane binding of IRSp53 upon cellular expression of HIV-1 Gag using membrane flotation assays (Figure 2c,d). In the absence of Gag ('HEK293T control' cells), one could observe the presence of IRSp53 both in the cytosol (Figure 2c, fractions 6–8, labeled with the ribosomal S6 biomarker) and in the cell membranes fractions (Figure 2c, fractions 1–3, labeled with the membrane Lamp2 biomarker). The lysosomal membrane protein Lamp2 and the cytosolic ribosomal protein S6 were used as controls to validate the correct separation of the membrane and cytosolic fractions. Thus, at equilibrium, 19 ± 8% of IRSp53 was bound to the cell membranes (Graph, Figure 2d). The same experiment was repeated with cells expressing HIV-1 Gag, where 66 ± 9% of Gag was bound to the cell membranes (Graph, Figure 2d). Notably, we observed a twofold increase with 44 ± 5% of IRSp53 bound to the cell membranes upon HIV-1 Gag expression (Graph Figure 2d) (n = 5 independent experiments, p value = 0.000129, Student's t-test), while none with IRTKS. This effect was comparable with the one of Tsg101, a protein of the ESCRT-I complex known to interact mainly with the p6 domain of Gag (Garrus et al., 2001; Pornillos et al., 2003; von Schwedler et al., 2003) and partially with the NC domain (El Meshri et al., 2018). The cellular endosomal sorting complex required for transport (ESCRT) machinery has been involved in the mechanism of vesicular budding of intracellular multi-vesicular bodies and also hijacked by the HIV-1 Gag protein for viral particle budding. Here, we observe a twofold increase in cell membrane binding of Tsg101 upon Gag expression, passing from 36 ± 10% without Gag to 79 ± 8% in the presence of Gag (Figure 2c) (n = 5 independent experiments, p value = 0.00517, Student's t-test).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a possible mechanism, referencing previous work showing Gag activates Rac1.
